open-question.question: How does the tool turn the first five words of the title into the kebab-case slug: what counts as a word, how are punctuation, apostrophes, digits, and non-ASCII letters handled, are stop words kept, and what happens when the result is empty?

Does the tool validate the value of --title (non-empty, a single line, a length cap, characters that would break the Markdown heading), and is the title written into the requirements.md heading verbatim or normalized?
open-question.alternative: Treat --title the way the open-question tool already treats a Short Title: collapse whitespace runs and newlines to one space, trim the ends, refuse the value only when it is empty after that fold, and write the folded title into the `# Milestone N: title` heading with its words, case and punctuation unchanged. There is no length cap and no character check. It reuses a rule the project already has, the `fold` helper plus the "the Short Title is empty" refusal in `open_questions.py`, so the two tools behave the same way. It removes the one real way a title can break the heading (an embedded newline) by repairing it rather than refusing it. It also keeps the model's chosen wording exactly, which the goal leaves as the model's only creative act. Some bad input is repaired silently instead of reported. A caller who passes a multi-line or badly spaced title gets a different heading than it sent and no signal. With no length cap, a run-on title lands in the heading as it is. Any slug built from the title's first words also sees the folded form.

Validate --title and refuse, with one Error: line, anything that is not already a clean heading title: empty or whitespace-only, containing a newline or other control character, longer than a fixed cap (for example 80 characters, above the longest existing title of 56), or ending in a space-then-`#` run that Markdown would strip as a closing sequence. A title that passes is written into the heading exactly as given. Nothing is ever changed silently. The heading is byte-for-byte what the caller passed, and every rejected case names its reason, which suits a headless chain where a quietly repaired title would go unnoticed. The cap and the closing-hash check also block the rare inputs that would render wrongly even after whitespace folding. It adds several validation rules, each needing its own test and its own error message, and the cap is an arbitrary number with no precedent in the project. A title the model chose reasonably (for example with a doubled space) fails the whole run instead of going through. That makes the skill's model redo work the tool could have done.

Fold and refuse-empty as in the first option, then also normalize the title's casing to one house style (for example sentence case) before writing the heading, so every tool-made heading follows the same convention. It ends the inconsistency the starting state records: the 37 existing headings mix Title Case (`Public Release Preparation`) and sentence case (`Non-interactive milestone activation`). Future headings stay uniform whatever casing the model happens to choose. Mechanical case conversion damages proper nouns, acronyms and mixed-case identifiers such as XML, SkillsBench or a file name, and the tool cannot tell those apart from ordinary words. The heading can then read worse than what the model wrote. The change also moves a stylistic judgment out of the skill, even though the goal leaves choosing the title as the model's work.

open-question.question: Is the milestones root a fixed path relative to the working directory or a tool argument, and when that root is missing does the tool create it or refuse, given that the bootstrap skill owns creating it?

Which directory names count in the milestone-number scan (only names shaped milestone_<digits>_<slug>, with non-digit prefixes ignored?), and how is the number zero-padded once it reaches three digits?

What counts as a conflict the tool refuses on, beyond the target directory already existing: a slug already used under another number, the same number under another slug, or a non-directory entry at the target path?
open-question.alternative: The only conflict check is creating the target directory exclusively (a create that fails if anything already sits at the path, rather than one that tolerates an existing directory). Any existing entry at `milestones/milestone_<NN>_<slug>`, whether a directory, a file, or a symlink, becomes the one `Error:` line. A slug reused under another number and the same number under another slug are both allowed. It is the smallest rule and the hardest to get wrong. The filesystem enforces it atomically, so no race between checking and creating is possible. With max-plus-one numbering, a clash can only come from an entry the scan missed, and this still catches every such entry at the exact target path. It also refuses before anything is written, so nothing is left behind. It drops the guard the skill has today: step 3 refuses a number already taken under any slug. An entry the scan ignores could then leave two milestones sharing one number, for example a stray `milestone_38_x` file, a differently padded `milestone_038_y`, or a non-matching name. Two directories with the same number would break `goto-next-milestone`'s lowest-undone pick and the history headings keyed on the number. How much this matters depends on which names the number scan counts.

Before writing, the tool refuses in two cases. The first is anything already at the target path, of any kind. The second is any entry in the milestones root, directory or not and under any padding, whose zero-stripped number equals the computed one under a different slug. Slug reuse under another number stays allowed. It keeps the skill's current number-uniqueness guarantee, which `goto-next-milestone` and the `### Milestone N — Title` history rely on to identify a milestone. It also closes the gap between what the scan counts and what exists on disk, and it adds no rule the workflow does not already need. Slug reuse is harmless because every consumer addresses a milestone by its full directory path or its number. It needs a second pass over the root with its own looser name matching, beside the number scan's matching, and the two must stay consistent. Under max-plus-one numbering this check almost never fires, so it is mostly defensive code that still needs its own tests and fixtures. Because it is a separate check before an exclusive create, it still needs the create to fail safely if something appears at the path in between.

This keeps both refusals from the target-path-and-number option and adds a third. The tool also refuses when the derived slug already names an existing milestone under any other number. Every milestone then has a unique number and a unique slug. A repeated slug is most likely a repeated or near-duplicate goal, and this surfaces it at definition time. It keeps directory names unambiguous to humans reading `milestones/` and git history, where the `Milestone-definition:` subjects would otherwise repeat a descriptor. None of the 37 existing slugs repeats, so the rule rejects nothing today. The slug is now derived mechanically from the title's first five words, so different goals with similar titles will collide, especially generic openings. The only fix is for the model to pick a different title, which adds a retry loop to a skill meant to be mechanical. That loop blocks a headless `claude -p` chain. How often it fires depends on how the slug normalization handles stop words and truncation.

open-question.question: How does define_milestone.py reach the open-question tool's code to create open_questions.xml: importing it as a sibling module located from its own file path, or running open_questions.py create as a subprocess?

When a failure happens after some files were written, what exactly does the tool remove (the files it wrote, the milestone directory it created, a milestones root it created) and what does it report when the cleanup itself fails?
open-question.alternative: The tool keeps a list of every path it creates in order: the milestones root if it had to create it, the milestone directory, then each of the four files. On any failure it removes them in reverse order, using a plain unlink for files and a non-recursive rmdir for directories, so it never removes anything it did not create. If the cleanup itself fails, the single Error: line gives the original reason and then the paths that could not be removed. It removes exactly what this run added and nothing else, including a milestones root created on a cold start. Using rmdir on the directories means a stray file some other process drops into them makes cleanup stop and report, not destroy that file. This keeps the goal's "leaves nothing behind" promise without going past the tool's own footprint. Every write step, including the one that creates open_questions.xml through the open-question tool's code, has to report the paths it created back to the tracker. That coupling is awkward if the open-question tool is run as a subprocess whose makedirs call does not say what it created. The root entry only matters if the tool creates the root instead of refusing when it is missing.

The tool refuses up front when the target milestone directory already exists, so on failure it treats that directory as entirely its own. It removes the directory recursively with rmtree and leaves the milestones root alone even if this run created it. If rmtree fails, the single Error: line adds the leftover directory path after the original reason. The cleanup is simple: one call, no per-file bookkeeping, and no need for the open-question code path to report what it created. Every file the tool writes lives inside that one directory, so this covers all of them. A recursive delete removes anything else that appears in the directory between creation and failure, which is a small race but a destructive one. Leaving a root the tool created (an empty milestones directory) falls short of a literal "leaves nothing behind" whenever the tool is allowed to create the root.

The tool builds the whole milestone in a hidden temporary directory under the milestones root: open_questions.xml through the open-question code, then the three Markdown files. It publishes the result with one os.rename to the final milestone_<NN>_<slug> name. Any failure before the rename removes only the temporary directory. If that removal fails, the Error: line names the leftover temporary path, which a later run can recognise and ignore in its number scan. The milestone path is created all at once or not at all. No other reader ever sees a half-written milestone directory, and the conflict check and the publish step meet at a single rename that fails if the target appears in the meantime. This extends the open-question tool's existing temp-file-then-rename pattern from one file to the whole directory. It is the most machinery for a tool that runs once per milestone. The number scan and the tests have to ignore leftover temporary directories. A cleanup failure leaves a hidden directory that is harder to spot than a visible partial milestone. It also does not cover a milestones root the tool creates itself, which still needs its own undo whenever the tool is allowed to create the root.

open-question.question: What exactly does the tool print on success: the order of the commit subject and the four file paths, whether each is on its own line with or without a label, and whether the paths are relative to the working directory or absolute?
Does the new tool mirror the open-question tool's stream and exit-status contract (one Error: line on stderr with exit 1, argparse usage with exit 2, empty stdout on failure, never a traceback)?
open-question.alternative: Give define_milestone.py its own main() and _fail() modelled on open_questions.py. It reconfigures stdout and stderr to UTF-8, maps ToolError and OSError to one folded Error: line on stderr with exit 1, and catches every other exception the same way so no traceback ever escapes. argparse keeps its usage message and exit 2, and stdout stays empty on every failure path. Both tools behave the same to every caller. The skill stops on an Error: line in both, test_contract.py's assertions can be copied into a sibling test file as they are, and the stdout-empty-on-failure rule means a partial success print (a subject or paths from the success output) can never reach the commit procedure after a failed run. The roughly fifteen lines of stream and exception handling exist twice, in two modules, with nothing that enforces they stay the same. If one tool's contract changes later (a new OSError folding rule, for example), the other can silently drift unless a test pins both.

Keep the contract exactly the same, but have define_milestone.py take the error-mapping entry point (the _fail helper and the ToolError/OSError/Exception handling in main) from open_questions.py instead of writing its own. The two tools then share one implementation of the stream and exit-status rules. By construction the contract cannot drift between the tools: one code path decides how an error is folded into a single line and which exit status it gets, so an OSError raised by the milestone scan reads the same as one raised inside create. This only works if the new tool imports the open-question module. If that reuse is done by running open_questions.py create as a subprocess instead, this option falls away. It also turns a private helper (_fail) and main's internals into an interface the second tool depends on, when the module docstring currently describes open_questions.xml as the one file this module owns.

alternative.id: Distinct exit status per failure class

open-question.alternative: Keep the streams the same (one Error: line on stderr, empty stdout on failure, argparse exit 2, never a traceback), but give each class of refusal its own non-zero status. For example: 1 for a conflict or invalid input, and a separate code for an I/O failure or for a failed cleanup that left files on disk. A headless chain (claude -p in ways-of-using-cairn.md) or a script could tell a harmless refusal, where nothing was written, from a case where the "leaves nothing behind" promise was broken, without parsing the Error: text. That distinction matters most when cleanup itself fails. It breaks the plugin's single tool contract and the rule every skill follows today of stopping on the Error: line whatever the status. The skill layer would never branch on the extra codes, so they are untested surface. How much they are worth depends on what the tool reports when cleanup fails, which is decided elsewhere.

open-question.question: Is the goal text read from stdin written under the Goal heading verbatim (newlines and blank lines preserved) or normalized, and is an empty, terminal, or non-UTF-8 stdin refused as the open-question tool refuses it?

Does the skill keep its single goal-description argument with the model deriving the title from it, or take a separate title argument, and does the headless invocation in ways-of-using-cairn.md change accordingly?

Does the new tool get its own pytest coverage under tests/ following the existing per-subcommand convention, with a second subprocess runner fixture in conftest.py and fixtures for milestone-root layouts, run under both interpreters and in CI?

Which surfaces that describe the plugin as shipping one Python tool (CLAUDE.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, the bootstrap's Python-check justification, docs/skill-reference.md, docs/workflow.md) are updated to name the second tool, and how?

Do the requirements.md, TASKS_TODO.md, and TASKS_DONE.md templates move out of the skill's prose into the tool source, so SKILL.md no longer states any file contents, or does the skill keep them as documentation?
